citation: "Chicago River." Wikipedia. Paraphrasing Lt. James Strode Swearingen's 1803 description of the river at Fort Dearborn, footnoted to its reprinting in Quaife 1913, and the 1833-37 harbour works after Holland and Andreas.
note: A finding aid, not evidence. What matters here is the figure it carries from Swearingen 1803: the river at Fort Dearborn about 30 yards (90 ft) wide and upwards of 18 ft deep, with banks 8 ft high on the south side and 6 ft on the north. Also: the pre-reversal flow was sluggish and outward into the lake with a near-zero surface gradient, which is what licenses a flat water surface at the datum through the whole downtown reach. Both figures are measured at the FORT, roughly 1.2 miles downstream of the forks — do not carry them to the forks without saying so. Chase Swearingen to a primary printing before promoting anything derived from it to documented. READ IN FULL 2026-08-11 AND IT IS NOT THE CASE THE OTHER TWO WERE. docs/STATUS.md § 44 listed this page beside chicagology_prefire062 and prefire276 as looking like a modern host carrying an old document. It is not one: the Swearingen material is a single sentence of Wikipedia's own prose — 'described the river as being about 30 yd wide and upwards of 18 ft deep at the place where the fort was intended to be built; the riverbanks were 8 ft high on the south side and 6 ft on the north' — carrying a footnote, not a quotation. No word of the journal is printed here. THE FOOTNOTE IS THE THING WORTH HAVING and it is the primary printing this record has been asking for since it was written: 'Journal of Lieutenant James Strode Swearingen reproduced in Quaife 1913, pp. 373-377' — Milo Milton Quaife, Chicago and the Old Northwest, 1673-1835 (University of Chicago Press, 1913). Fetch those five pages and the figures stop resting on an encyclopedia. THE FLAT-WATER SENTENCE IS WEAKER STILL, and it is the one this dataset actually stands on. The claim that licenses a level water surface is Wikipedia's 'the Chicago River flowed sluggishly into Lake Michigan from Chicago's flat plain', in the Reversing-the-flow section, where the only footnote in reach is to a 1998 geological survey paper about the ice-age ridge. So the `documented` grade on the ground `water` claim in terrain_spec.json rests on unfootnoted encyclopedia prose and not on Swearingen at all — see docs/RESEARCH/evidence_tiers_round_two.md § 4.
carries_no_document: Opened and read in full 2026-08-11 (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chicago_River&action=raw, HTTP 200). Looked for a transcription of Swearingen's 1803 journal and there is none: the page paraphrases him in one sentence of its own prose and footnotes the reprinting, which is a citation and not a reprinting. Every other passage this project draws on here is the same shape. So this record's rung is a judgement about an encyclopedia article — later scholarship, tier 4 — and the documents behind it have to be fetched on their own terms. Where it sends you: Quaife 1913, pp. 373-377 for Swearingen; Holland, Chicago in Maps (2005), pp. 102-109 and Andreas vol. 1, pp. 234-235 for the harbour works.
